lede: Push something heavy and it shifts slowly; push something light with the same effort and it shoots away. Newton's second law puts a number on that. Unit 2 uses it on boxes dragged along a floor, often by a rope at an angle, and on lifts hanging from a cable.
can: Find the resultant force along the line of motion and use it in $F = ma$
Put the mass in the equation and the weight on the diagram
Split a pull at an angle into the part that drives and the part that lifts

text: Force, mass and the motion that follows

md: Forces do not make things move at a steady speed; they make things change speed. The bigger the resultant force and the lighter the body, the faster that change happens, and one short equation says exactly how much.

text: 1. The resultant is what goes in

caption: A box pulled by $100$ N against $20$ N of resistance; the dashed arrow is the acceleration, not a force.

md:
$F = ma$ is on the Unit 2 sheet, and the $F$ is the **resultant** along the line of motion. Here that is $100 - 20 = 80$ N.

Then $80 = 16a$ gives $a = 5$ m/s². The dashed arrow marks the acceleration, and it is deliberately drawn differently: it is not a force.

prompt: A trolley is pushed by 55 N against a resistance of 15 N. What resultant force goes into $F = ma$, in newtons?
explain: The resultant is what the push has left once the resistance, acting backwards, is taken off it, just as the box above had 100 N take away 20 N. Here that is $55 - 15 = 40$ N.

text: 2. The mass goes in, not the weight

md: The 16 kg box weighs $16 \times 10 = 160$ N: that is the arrow pointing down on the diagram. The $m$ in $F = ma$ is the mass, in kilograms.
For the box above, $80 = 16a$ gives $5$ m/s². Put the weight in its place, $80 = 160a$, and you get $0.5$ m/s²: ten times too small, the slip the 2019 report found on this step.

title: Why the two cannot be swapped
md: Mass is how much matter there is; weight is how hard gravity pulls on it. $F = ma$ asks how hard a body is to accelerate, which depends on the matter, so the mass belongs in it.

prompt: A block of mass 4 kg, weight 40 N, feels a resultant force of 24 N. What is its acceleration, in m/s²?
explain: The $m$ in $F = ma$ is how much matter there is, the mass in kilograms, just as the box above used 16 and not 160. So $24 = 4a$ and $a = 6$ m/s²; dividing by the weight, 40, would give 0.6.

md:
**A 15 kg crate dragged by 75 N against 30 N.**
**Line 1:** *for the crate*, with the direction of motion positive.
**Line 2:** resultant $= 75 - 30 = 45$ N
**Line 3:** $45 = 15a$
**Line 4:** $a = 3$ m/s²

Naming the body keeps one body's forces apart from a whole system's, which the 2019 report saw mixed up. Line 3 is a method mark that survives an arithmetic slip, so write it even when the numbers look awkward.

title: Newton's 2nd Law of Motion, F = ma
why: The same law at a slower pace, with the resultant formed before anything else. It is an A level video, so stop before any coefficient of friction appears: CCEA never uses one.

prompt: A crate of mass 10 kg is dragged by 80 N against a resistance of 30 N. What is its acceleration, in m/s²?
explain: The same four lines as the crate above: name the body, form the resultant, $80 - 30 = 50$ N, then $50 = 10a$, so $a = 5$ m/s².

md: CCEA never tests $F = \mu R$. Friction arrives either as a plain value or as **so many newtons per kilogram**, and the second form is a one-step conversion: multiply by the mass. It looks like a coefficient and it is not one.

**Resistance:** a 14 kg trolley at $2$ N per kg feels $2 \times 14 = 28$ N.
**Equation:** pushed by 70 N, $70 - 28 = 14a$
**So:** $a = 3$ m/s². The conversion is its own line, and it carries its own mark.

prompt: A resistance of 3 N per kg acts on a sledge of mass 15 kg. What is the resisting force, in newtons?
explain: Per kilogram means every kilogram of the body is resisted by that much, so multiply by the mass, as the trolley above did: $3 \times 15 = 45$ N.

md:
Vertical motion is the same equation with the weight in it. Choose a direction, say so, and write the resultant in that direction.

**Up positive:** $7560 - 7000 = 700a$, so $a = 0.8$ m/s². The answer is positive, so the acceleration is upwards. A negative answer would simply mean downwards.

task: On the Acceleration screen, set friction to zero and apply a known force to a known mass. Predict the acceleration from $F = ma$ before you release, then check the readout. Turn friction on and predict again: the resultant is now the applied force minus the friction. The model is horizontal only, so it says nothing about the lift.

prompt: A lift of mass 300 kg hangs on a cable with tension 3300 N. Taking up as positive, which equation is right?
explain: With up positive, the tension counts plus and the weight counts minus, as in the lift above. The weight is the mass times $g$, $300 \times 10 = 3000$ N, so the equation is $3300 - 3000 = 300a$. Leaving the weight out, or taking off the mass instead, are the two usual slips.

md: A rope at an angle $\theta$ above the floor does two jobs at once. Its part along the floor, $P\cos\theta$, drives the box; its part upwards, $P\sin\theta$, lifts a little of the box's weight. Only the first goes into $F = ma$, because the box moves along the floor.

**Shown:** a 30 N rope at 20°.
**Along the floor:** $30\cos 20° = 28.19$ N, the side next to the angle.
**Straight up:** $30\sin 20° = 10.26$ N, the side opposite it.

prompt: A rope pulls a sledge with 20 N at 30° above the horizontal. What is the part of the pull along the ground, in newtons, to 2 decimal places?
explain: The part along the ground is the side of the triangle next to the angle, so it takes the cosine, as $P\cos\theta$ does in the picture: $20\cos 30° = 17.32$ N. The sine gives 10 N, the part that lifts.

md:
**Vertically, nothing accelerates:** $R + 30\sin 20° = 60$, so $R = 49.74$ N.
**Along the floor:** $30\cos 20° - 8 = 6a$
**So:** $20.19 = 6a$, giving $a = 3.37$ m/s².

The rope carries part of the weight, so the floor pushes back with less than the whole weight. Writing $R$ as the weight, or as the rope's upward part on its own, lost the reaction marks in 2019 and 2023.

prompt: A 4 kg block on a level floor is pulled along by a string at 30° above the horizontal with a tension of 10 N. What is the normal reaction, in newtons?
explain: Vertically nothing accelerates, so the reaction and the string's upward part together hold up the weight, as for the 6 kg box above. The upward part is $10\sin 30° = 5$ N, so $R + 5 = 40$ and $R = 35$ N.

md: **Show that** (2022, 2024, 2026). A value is printed for you to reach. Form the equation with the letter in it and solve forwards. Putting the printed value in and checking earned nothing in 2022 and at most two marks in 2024.

**Shown:** a lift of mass $M$ pulled up by 5460 N at 0.5 m/s², where you must show $M = 520$.
**Up positive:** $5460 - 10M = 0.5M$
**Collect:** $5460 = 10.5M$, so $M = 520$. The printed value arrives last.

prompt: A part says 'Show that the mass of the lift is 520 kg'. Which route earns full marks?
options: Forming the equation of motion and solving it for the mass
Putting 520 into the equation and showing both sides agree
Writing down 520 kg with its units
answer: Forming the equation of motion and solving it for the mass
explain: A show-that is marked on the derivation: the equation built from the forces with $M$ still in it, the $M$ terms collected, then solved, exactly as the lift above reached 520 on its last line. So forming and solving earns every mark; putting the value in and checking is verification, capped at two marks.

md: **Something changes** (2022, 2023). A later part swaps the box, the pull or the friction. First line: the equation again, with the new mass or force in every place it appears.
**How fast, or how far** (2019). The acceleration you found goes into a constant-acceleration formula. First line: list $u$, $a$ and $t$, with $u = 0$ when it starts from rest.

**At a steady speed** (2023). Constant velocity means no acceleration, so there is no $ma$ at all: the pull's part along the floor equals the friction. For 40 N at 20°: $40\cos 20° - F = 0$, so $F = 37.59$ N.

prompt: A block is dragged along a rough floor by a rope and moves at a constant velocity. What is the resultant force on the block?
options: Zero, so the forces along the floor balance
The rope's pull along the floor
answer: Zero, so the forces along the floor balance
explain: Constant velocity means the speed is not changing, so $a = 0$ and the resultant is $m \times 0 = 0$: the forces along the floor balance, as the 40 N pull and its friction did above. In 2023 many looked for an acceleration here that was not there.

md:
Form the resultant along the line of motion before using $F = ma$.
Put the mass in the equation and the weight on the diagram.
Turn a resistance per kilogram into one force, and write a lift's equation with its direction.
Split a pull at an angle: $P\cos\theta$ drives, $P\sin\theta$ lightens the reaction.
Spot the twists: a show-that, a change of load, a formula after, a steady speed.

When this has a question of its own (Q3 in 2019, 2022 and 2023) it is a block on a level floor, often pulled at an angle: the forces, the normal reaction, the acceleration, then a change or a formula after. The equation earns one mark for the resultant along the floor and one for $= ma$. Stuck? Write *for the block:*, then resolve the pull.
